title: Pauri 10: listening, truth and contentment
hook: suniai: by listening come truth, contentment and wisdom, worth bathing at every shrine (Japji 10)
tomorrow: Pauri 11: listening, the blind find the way

segments.voice: Yesterday, pauri nine: by listening, even the bad-mouthed turn to praise. Your line was the lowly speak praise. Did you hear something good from someone unexpected? Day one hundred eighty.

There's a moment most of us know. You're scrolling through something you might buy, a jacket, a phone, a trip, and you already have one that works perfectly well. You know it. And still there's a little tug: but this one's better. The tug never quite goes away; there's always a next one. Now think of the rare moments when the tug stops. A meal with friends where nobody checks the time. A quiet evening when nothing is missing. Pauri ten has a name for that feeling, and says where it comes from.
screen: `BUT THIS ONE'S BETTER.` → `THE TUG THAT NEVER STOPS.` → `WHEN NOTHING IS MISSING.`

segments.voice: Here is pauri ten in plain words, following Macauliffe. By listening come truth, contentment and divine knowledge. By listening, the bath at the sixty-eight places of pilgrimage. By listening, reading and reading, honor is won. By listening, the mind settles easily into meditation. Nanak, the devotees are always in bloom. By listening, pain and wrongdoing are wiped away. The first line is the heart of it: suniai sat santokh giaan. Sat is truth, the same root as sach. Giaan is knowledge, wisdom. And in the middle, today's word: santokh. Contentment. Enough. Not giving up, not pretending not to want anything. It's the settled feeling of having enough, the tug gone quiet. Sikh teaching often counts santokh among the great virtues, alongside truth, compassion, humility and love. Notice where the pauri says it comes from: listening. Not from getting the next thing, and not from grimly denying yourself. From hearing the Name until the restless wanting loosens its grip on its own. Then that second line: the sixty-eight places of pilgrimage. Indian tradition counted sixty-eight great bathing places, and people walked for months to reach them. Remember pauri six, the bath that's only worth it if it pleases Him. Here Guru Nanak says it plainly: listening is the bath at all sixty-eight at once. And the last line before the refrain: sahaj dhiaan. Sahaj is ease, naturalness. The meditation that comes without forcing. Contentment and ease, by listening. You don't have to wrestle the tug down. You listen, and it quiets.
screen: `SAT, SANTOKH, GIAAN.` · `SANTOKH — ENOUGH.` · `THE SIXTY-EIGHT SHRINES AT ONCE.` · `SAHAJ — MEDITATION WITH EASE.` · then, large: `ENOUGH, BY LISTENING.`

segments.voice: Pick one thing in front of you, or in your life, exactly as it is. Your chair. Your hands. The light in the room. This day, as it's gone so far. Don't improve it in your head. Don't compare it to a better version. Just let it be enough, for the length of the bell. When the tug comes, and it will, notice it, and go back to listening: to your breath, to the room. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Santokh. Contentment, the settled sense of enough. Japji's tenth pauri says it comes by listening.
Your line: enough, by listening. The next time you feel the tug to buy or add something today, wait one full minute and just listen to what's around you. Day one hundred eighty.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite the tenth pauri each morning; santokh, contentment, is often taught as one of five virtues, with sat (truth), daya (compassion), nimrata (humility) and pyaar (love).

match.prompt: what's inside the pauri — tap the pairs.

myth: santokh means giving up all wanting by force
it's the settled sense of enough, which comes by listening, not by grim denial.
the pauri says listening is worth a bath at sixty-eight shrines
santokh is counted among the great Sikh virtues
with truth, compassion, humility and love.

fork.setup: you want contentment, the feeling of enough. where does pauri ten say it comes from?
fork.reveal: suniai sat santokh giaan: by listening come truth, contentment and wisdom, and listening is itself the bath at all sixty-eight shrines.

original.note: Gurmukhi: santokh, contentment. from pauri 10: ਸੁਣਿਐ ਸਤੁ ਸੰਤੋਖੁ ਗਿਆਨੁ.

trapdoor: what it means: contentment, the settled sense of enough, which Japji says comes by listening.
what a scholar hears: santokh comes from Sanskrit santosha; later in Japji, contentment appears beside dharma in the line about what keeps the earth in its place.

sources.ref: Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), vol. 1, the Japji, pauri 10

notes: Pauri 10 paraphrased after Macauliffe; not quoted.
Sixty-eight tirthas (athsath tirath) as the traditional count of great pilgrimage places: confirm.
The five virtues (sat, santokh, daya, nimrata, pyaar) as a standard Sikh list: confirm.
Trapdoor teases pauri 16 (santokh thaap rakhiaa jin soot), taught on day 188. Confirm.

Reviewer edit: the trapdoor no longer calls contentment 'the thread that holds the earth'; pauri 16 is read variously (dharma as the bull, contentment as what holds it in place, or dharma born of compassion patiently holding the earth). Also softened 'the five virtues' to 'often taught as one of five virtues', since lists vary.
